chapter_en: Maintaining a Synagogue: Objects of Holiness and of Mitzva

sections.title_en: 1. The Prohibition of Breaking Anything from the Synagogue
sections.body_en:
The holiness of the synagogue, which is called a 'small sanctuary', is akin to the holiness of the Temple (above 13:1), and just as it is forbidden to demolish anything from the Temple or the altar, as it is said (Devarim 12:4): "You shall not do so to the Lord your God" – so it is forbidden to demolish anything from the synagogue (Mordekhai; Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 152:1). Included in this, one must take care not to peel paint off the wall of the synagogue absent-mindedly.

But anything that is for the needs of the synagogue is permitted, because this is not demolition but the repair of the synagogue's needs. Therefore it is permitted to peel off the paint in order to whitewash the synagogue anew, and it is permitted to pull up old floor tiles in order to replace them with new ones. Likewise it is permitted to drill into the walls of the synagogue in order to pass electric wires through them or to install an air-conditioning or alarm system. And likewise it is permitted to drill into them in order to attach to them lamps, cupboards, electric sockets, a charity box, memorial boards and anything that it is customary to do in the synagogue (Rambam, Foundations of the Torah 6:7; Rema, Oraḥ Ḥayim 152:1; Eliya Rabba; Mishna Berura 12).

Likewise, it is permitted to reduce the space of the synagogue in order to beautify it, such as covering its walls with marble or wood, or fixing along its sides fine bookcases and compartments for people's needs, for anything done for the beauty of the synagogue or for the needs of its accepted uses – is permitted (Divrei Ḥayim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:4).

The outer walls of the synagogue too are included in the prohibition of demolition; therefore one must take care not to crumble the plaster that covers them on the outside, and likewise one must take care not to kick the wall of the synagogue absent-mindedly, lest one knock off a little of the plaster on the outside.1

It is permitted to install solar panels for producing electricity on the roof of the synagogue, for since the income from this will be dedicated to running the synagogue, there is no prohibition of demolition in drilling the holes for installing them. And there is no affront to the honour of the synagogue in using its roof, since the synagogue benefits from it. However, one must take care to place the panels in a way that will not make the synagogue ugly and harm its honour. Ideally one should not drill into the outer side of the synagogue wall for other needs; however, when there is a need to make use of it in order to pass electricity or communication lines, as long as it does not make the synagogue ugly and harm its honour, it is permitted. For it was with this understanding that the synagogue was built, that in time of need its outer walls could be made use of.2

notes_en.en:
Sifrei Devarim (Re'eh 61): "From where do we know that one who demolishes a single stone from the Heikhal, from the altar or from the courtyards transgresses a negative commandment? The verse says: 'And you shall break down their altars and shatter their pillars… You shall not do so to the Lord your God'". The Mordekhai wrote (Megilla 826): "The synagogue is called a small sanctuary, and therefore it is forbidden to demolish anything from the synagogue… And if one demolished in order to build, it is permitted, for that demolition is called building". And the Beit Yosef brought it (Oraḥ Ḥayim 151:10). Above 12:3, note 1, we learned that some hold that the holiness of the synagogue is from the Torah, and consequently the prohibition of demolishing it is from the Torah. However, according to most poskim the holiness of the synagogue is rabbinic, and consequently the prohibition of demolishing it is also rabbinic (so explained Torat Ḥesed 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 4; Avnei Nezer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 34-35; Sedei Ḥemed, Ma'arekhet Bet 43, and others. However, according to the Ḥesed Le-Avraham, Te'omim, Tinyana, Oraḥ Ḥayim 14, even according to those who hold that the holiness of a synagogue is from the Torah, the prohibition of demolishing it is rabbinic. On the other hand, according to the Divrei Ḥayim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:3, even according to those who hold that the holiness of the synagogue is rabbinic, the prohibition of demolishing it is from the Torah. And see Shevet Ha-Levi 3:13). And it appears that if the demolition is done in a disrespectful manner, according to all views there is in it a Torah prohibition of neglecting the mitzva of the fear of God (as explained above 12:3, note 1). And as the Responsa Beit Yitzḥak wrote (Even Ha-Ezer 2:33), that even according to those who hold that the holiness of the synagogue is rabbinic, the prohibition of disgracing it is from the Torah. And so wrote the Heikhal Yitzḥak (Oraḥ Ḥayim 12).
Destroying objects of holiness (below halakhot 8-10): The Magen Avraham wrote (154:9) that one who destroys 'objects of holiness' too transgresses the Torah prohibition of 'You shall not do so'. And according to the Ḥikrei Lev (second edition, Yoreh De'ah 10), its prohibition is rabbinic. And as stated, it appears that he too would agree that in a disrespectful manner it is forbidden by the Torah (Gedulei Ha-Kodesh 282:3. And similarly in Kiryat Sefer on the Rambam, Torah Scroll 10:4; Ha-Elef Lekha Shlomo, Oraḥ Ḥayim 77).

The Taz wrote (151:3) that those people who make a hole in the wall of the synagogue in order to rest the shelf of their lectern in it, although they benefit from it, are not acting properly, for they are demolishing the synagogue. And so wrote Ḥayei Adam (17:10) and the Ben Ish Ḥai (Vayikra 16). And most poskim did not accept his words, for anything that is for a need – is permitted (Eliya Rabba; Mateh Yehuda; Mishna Berura 152:12; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 5, and others). And it is possible that even the Taz, who was stringent, intended a private person who made a hole in the wall for his own comfort, while harming the beauty of the synagogue, and with this perhaps all agree. However, what the gabbaim do in a fine manner for the benefit of the synagogue and all the worshippers – is permitted according to all views (Aryeh De-Vei Ilai, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2; Ḥavatzelet Ha-Sharon 1:1). When there is a need to reduce the bima or the Holy Ark in order to add seats, it is permitted to do so, while taking care that the beauty of the synagogue is not harmed (see Yeshu'at Moshe 1:27; Minḥat Yitzḥak, Likkutei Teshuvot 15).
Sometimes there is a need to break a wall in the synagogue in order to open windows to the women's section or in order to make stairs to the women's section. In principle, anything that is for the need of the synagogue is permitted, but a doubt arose whether the women's section is considered sanctified, so as to demolish for its sake in the synagogue itself (see above 12:11, note 10). And therefore they suggested that the 'seven good men of the town' (below 6) sell the place that needs to be demolished, and then demolish what is needed (the Ḥiddushei Ha-Rim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2; Divrei Ḥayim, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:13; Avnei Nezer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 33; Divrei Malkiel 5:11). Similarly there were some who ruled so, to remove all doubt, in further cases of doubt (Heikhal Yitzḥak 1:13; Minḥat Shlomo 2:4; Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:47). And it appears that if it is clear to the gabbaim that the breaking is within the purposes of the synagogue, and the public relies on them, it is permitted even without a sale, since they have the status of 'the good men of the town'. And perhaps the rabbis who ruled to sell were concerned that the good men of the town would give in to the forceful people in the community and make a decision that is not for the honour of the synagogue and the worshippers; but after they sell, the holiness will lapse from the structure, and consequently they will not transgress a possible prohibition of demolition.

sections.body_en:
Just as it is forbidden to demolish anything from the synagogue, so it is forbidden to damage the furniture of the synagogue, such as benches, tables and cupboards, and all the more so the Holy Ark and the bima. Included in this, one must take care not to peel the paint off the benches and tables of the synagogue absent-mindedly, and not to carve needless engravings into them (Mishna Berura 152:11).

It is permitted to borrow from the synagogue chairs and portable tables for a meal and the like, on condition that they are not distinctive furniture of the synagogue, that the borrowing is with the permission of the gabbaim, and that no disturbance to the prayer will result from it (Maharam Padua 65; Biur Halakha 152, s.v. 'Ve-asur'). But benches and tables that are distinctive furniture of the synagogue and part of its beauty have the law of the synagogue, and they should not be lent for a weekday purpose.3

notes_en.en: The Ḥatam Sofer (on Shulḥan Arukh 152:1) and the Mishna Berura (152:11; Biur Halakha, s.v. 'Lisstor') wrote that the prohibition of demolition applies also to the benches of the synagogue. And so wrote the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (154:12), but he permitted lending them by virtue of the principle that 'the court stipulates' ('lev beit din matneh'). However, in the Peri Megadim (Eshel Avraham 152:6) he wrote that the benches of the synagogue do not have the law of a synagogue. And it appears that if it is a distinctive piece of furniture of the synagogue, such as benches characteristic of the synagogue, their law is like that of the synagogue itself, that the prohibition of demolition applies to them and they should not be lent. But portable chairs and tables that are not intended specifically for the synagogue, and from the outset it is clear to all that they can be used also for weekday purposes – do not have the law of the synagogue.

sections.body_en:
The Sages forbade demolishing or selling a synagogue before another is built in its place (Megilla 26b). That is to say, even when there is a clear plan and cash in hand for building a larger synagogue, and in the meantime they have a temporary place to pray in, it is forbidden to destroy the synagogue in order to build another in its place, lest some mishap befall them and they be forced to use the money intended for building the synagogue for other needs, and they remain without a synagogue. Rather, only after they finish building the new synagogue may they demolish the old one or sell it (Bava Batra 3b; Shulḥan Arukh 152:1; Mishna Berura 2; 5). And if they have a permanent synagogue in which they can pray comfortably in the meantime, in case of need they may demolish the old synagogue before they build the new one. And this is the advice for worshippers who wish to build on the site of their old synagogue a new, finer synagogue: that they find a permanent place where they can pray comfortably and without restriction until they finish building the synagogue, and then they can demolish the old one and build the new one in its place.

If cracks appeared in the walls of the synagogue and there is concern that it will collapse – they should demolish it at once, and hasten to build a new synagogue with work as continuous as possible, so that they can soon return to pray in it. It is related of Rav Ashi, who was one of the great Amoraim and also merited wealth, that he saw cracks in the walls of the synagogue in his town, and out of concern for the lives of the worshippers he commanded that it be demolished and rebuilt. And so that they would not delay its building, he moved his bed to the site of the synagogue, and did not return to sleep in his house until they finished building it (Bava Batra 3b; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 152:1).

When there is a need to enlarge the synagogue, they should first build the new wall, and only afterwards dismantle the old wall, so that there will not be a moment in which the synagogue is not built and closed on its four sides. In a pressing situation, when it is not possible to carry out the work in this way, it is permitted first to dismantle the existing wall and to build the new wall as quickly as possible (Biur Halakha there, s.v. 'Dina', following the view of the Rosh and the Rambam).4

In a pressing situation, when they must enlarge the synagogue because it is too small to hold all the worshippers, and there is no way to enlarge it without first demolishing it – having no choice, it is permitted to demolish it and rebuild it at once, even when in the meantime they will have to pray in a temporary place.5

notes_en.en:
The law of selling is like the law of demolishing: it is forbidden to sell a synagogue before they buy or build another in its place (Biur Halakha 152, s.v. 'Ein'; Oraḥ Mishpat 151). And likewise concerning renting: they should not cancel the rental of a place that serves as a synagogue before they rent another place (Mishna Berura 3). The law of a study hall in this matter is like the law of a synagogue (Peri Megadim; Mishna Berura 152:1).
According to the Rosh, the Beit Yosef, the Magen Avraham (152:1) and the Rav Pe'alim (Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:20), even if there is a permanent synagogue there that can hold everyone without crowding, it is forbidden to demolish a synagogue before they build another in its place, lest they be negligent in building it. However, according to Tosafot (Bava Batra 3b, s.v. 'Bei Kaita'), the Ramban, the Rashba, the Ran, the Nimukei Yosef, the Taz, the Gra (152:1) and others, the concern is lest they be delayed in building the synagogue and in those days remain without a synagogue; but if they have a permanent and spacious synagogue in which they can pray in the meantime, it is permitted, for there is no need to be concerned that the public will be negligent forever and not build the synagogue. And so is the halakha, since the prohibition is rabbinic and it is a need of a mitzva (Biur Halakha 152, s.v. 'She-lo'). And so I wrote above.
When cracks appeared in the synagogue and there is no way to stabilise it without demolishing it, even if it can hold out for several more years, it is permitted to demolish it at once and hasten to build it as quickly as possible, for perhaps if they postpone it, in the future they will not have money for it (Responsa Ḥatam Sofer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 34; Da'at Torah 152, in the name of Responsa Aryeh De-Vei Ilai, Oraḥ Ḥayim 3).

Just as they were lenient in a situation where there are cracks in the wall, so one should be lenient in a pressing situation when there is not room for all the worshippers (Rosh, Bava Batra 1:4; Aryeh De-Vei Ilai, Oraḥ Ḥayim 3; Biur Halakha 152, s.v. 'She-lo'; Maharsham 5:1, s.v. 'U-ve-ikar').
Some say that in every case of doubt it is good to demolish through a gentile, for in this way it is a 'shevut de-shevut' (Beit Shlomo, Oraḥ Ḥayim 23; Torat Ḥesed, Oraḥ Ḥayim 4:7; Levushei Mordekhai, Oraḥ Ḥayim Tinyana 25). In practice, it appears that one should not seek out a gentile to destroy the synagogue, for there is in this an aspect of desecration of God's Name (see Maharsham 5:1; 61), and when it has been ruled that it is permitted to demolish for the need of a mitzva, a Jew may do it. Moreover, even the advice to demolish through a gentile is not simple, for some say that apart from the melakhot of Shabbat, in all prohibitions a 'shevut de-shevut' is forbidden even for the need of a mitzva (Responsa Ḥatam Sofer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 32), and some say that when the gentile is the Jew's worker, it is not considered a shevut (see Maḥaneh Efrayim, Laws of Agents and Partners 11). And it appears that only when the Jew has gentile workers in any case is it preferable that they demolish.

sections.title_en: 4. Raising in Holiness When Selling Holy Objects
sections.body_en:
It is permitted to sell something holy in order to buy with the money received for it something holier, but not in order to buy something whose holiness is of a lower level, for the Sages stated a rule: "One raises in holiness and does not lower" (Menaḥot 99a; Shulḥan Arukh 153:1-4; Mishna Berura 11). In case of need one may sell even in order to buy something of the same level of holiness, as explained in the next halakha.6

The order of the levels from the bottom up: a synagogue, a study hall, the bima on which the Torah scroll is placed, the Holy Ark, mantles and coverings for covering the Torah scroll, printed sacred books, Ḥumashim and books of the Prophets or Writings written in ink on parchment, and above them all the Torah scroll (Megilla 26a; Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 153:1-2; Mishna Berura 6).

The permission to sell something holy in order to buy other holy things in its place is when the public has no need of it; but if the public would lack it, it is forbidden to sell it even in order to buy something holier than it (Ramban and Ritva, Megilla 25b; Rema 153:7).7

notes_en.en: In the Gemara Menaḥot (99a), we learned from the description of the erecting of the Mishkan that one does not lower a thing from its holiness, and from 'the firepans of these sinners' of the congregation of Koraḥ we learned that one raises in holiness, and therefore "let them make of them beaten plates as a covering for the altar, for they offered them before the Lord, and they became holy" (Bamidbar 17:3) – "at first they were accessories of the altar, and now they are the body of the altar itself". Some hold that this rule, 'one raises in holiness and does not lower', is from the Torah (Penei Yehoshua, Megilla 26a; Da'at Torah 153:3; Maḥaneh Ḥayim 1:1; Maharam Schick, Oraḥ Ḥayim 24). And some hold that it is rabbinic, and the verses brought in the Gemara are an asmakhta (Peri Megadim, Mishbetzot Zahav, introduction to siman 153, and likewise in his book Rosh Yosef, Megilla 25b; Yeshu'ot Ya'akov 153:1; Yehuda Ya'aleh 1:293). However, it appears that even according to those who are stringent, the holiness of the money received from selling objects of holiness is rabbinic, for the Ran wrote (on the Rif, Megilla 8a) that the holiness of the proceeds is lighter than the holiness of the holy objects. And so wrote the Ginat Veradim (Oraḥ Ḥayim 2:31) and the Maharash Engel (4:96). And in the Shulḥan Arukh Ha-Rav (Oraḥ Ḥayim 34:9) he wrote that the Torah prohibition applies only to the consecrated property of the Temple, concerning which there is a Torah prohibition of me'ila.

The Ramban wrote (Megilla 25b) that the permission to sell a synagogue in order to buy something holier, or for the sake of Torah study or the marriage of poor people, is only when the public has another synagogue that suffices for all their needs. Similarly wrote the Rashba (there 26b), the Ritva, the Beit Yosef (153:9), the Rema (there 7), the Leḥem Mishneh (Prayer 11:14) and the Taz (153:4; 12). (And see the Magen Avraham 153:7, and what the Peri Megadim wrote on him, Eshel Avraham 3, Mishbetzot Zahav 4; Biur Halakha 13, s.v. 'Lo yimkeru'.)
Similar to the law of selling objects of holiness, one should not change an object of holiness of a high level into an object of a level lower than it. However, to the same level of holiness it is permitted to change it in case of need; for example, when there is a need to make the Holy Ark smaller, because part of it broke or in order to add seats in the synagogue, it is permitted to make a small Holy Ark out of a large Holy Ark (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 154:6; Yoreh De'ah 282:13).
An object of holiness that can no longer serve its function: according to the view of the Taz (154:7), it is better to use it for a lighter holiness than to put it in geniza, just as worn-out mantles of books are used as shrouds for a met mitzva. And some disputed his words and ruled to put it in geniza (Bekhor Shor, Megilla 26b; Rav Pe'alim part 2, Oraḥ Ḥayim 20).
It is right to be stringent that even an individual who sells his own objects of holiness should use their proceeds to raise in holiness, and in case of need he may buy at the same level of holiness (as explained in the next halakha). For example, if he sold old sacred books – he should buy tefillin with them, and in case of need new sacred books; or if he sold kosher tefillin he should buy with their proceeds mehudarot ones. And in a pressing situation one may rely on the lenient view, that an individual with his own property is considered like 'the seven good men of the town' (as explained below in halakha 6), and he has the power to sell objects of holiness with the understanding that the money received from them will be ḥullin (see Shulḥan Arukh 153:10; Mishna Berura 62).
Obviously a scribe of Torah scrolls, tefillin and mezuzot, or a merchant of objects of holiness, may use the proceeds he received from their sale for ḥullin, for with this understanding he wrote or acquired them (Taz 153:10; Mishna Berura 62).
If a Torah scroll was stolen and the insurance paid its value, there is no obligation to use the compensation money for something holy, for it is not the money of its purchase but insurance benefits (Tzitz Eliezer 18:67).
In addition to the fact that with the money received for the holy object one must buy something holier, the holy object itself, such as the Holy Ark or the books of the Prophets, remains in its holiness, and the one who buys it must use it for its holy purpose. Except for a synagogue, which, if they sold it, goes out to ḥullin (as explained in halakha 6). However, in a pressing situation, some say that 'the seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town' (see below halakha 6) may decide that the object of holiness goes out to ḥullin; for example, the silver crown that adorned the Torah scroll wore out, and they want to sell it for melting down for weekday needs and to use the payment received for public needs that have no holiness (Ra'avad, Tamim De'im 115; Responsa of the Rosh 5:1; Tur, Yoreh De'ah 282:16; Levush, Oraḥ Ḥayim 153:9; Ḥatam Sofer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 38). And their reason is that the holiness of these objects is rabbinic, and in case of need the Sages gave permission to 'the seven good men of the town' to take their proceeds out to ḥullin. Furthermore, since it is customary to sell them, it is as though they consecrated them from the outset with this understanding. And some say that whenever they used the money for a holy need, even without the seven good men of the town the holiness lapsed from the objects of holiness, and it is permitted to take them out to ḥullin (Rambam, Torah Scroll 10:4, and Kesef Mishneh there; Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 282:16). On the other hand, some say that only over a synagogue, which is an object of mitzva, do the seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town have authority, but not over objects of holiness, like the law of consecrated objects that have already been used, which cannot be redeemed (Ramban and Ritva, Megilla 25a; Rashba there 27b; Ran there 8a in the pages of the Rif; Magen Avraham 153:14; Eliya Rabba 17; Gra 31; Mishna Berura 37; Ḥayei Adam 17:26). In practice, ideally one should not be lenient in this, and in a pressing situation, for example when the objects of holiness that were sold have no other use, one may be lenient (Ḥesed Le-Avraham, Te'omim, Oraḥ Ḥayim Tinyana 16).

sections.title_en: 5. Selling in Order to Buy at the Same Level of Holiness
sections.body_en:
The permission to sell something holy that is not needed, in order to buy in its place something holier than it, applies even ideally (Perisha; Eliya Rabba; Mishna Berura 153:3). But in order to buy something holy of the same level – ideally one should not sell, and in case of need it is permitted. For example, when the synagogue is too small to hold the worshippers, since there is a need in this, it is permitted to sell it in order to buy a large synagogue in its place. And they should do it simultaneously, so that there will not be a moment in which they remain without a synagogue, as explained in halakha 3 (Mishna Berura 153:11).8

A Torah scroll, since it is the holiest of all, may never be sold. Only in a pressing situation, when there is no possibility of maintaining Torah study, or when there is no possibility of marrying off poor people or of redeeming a captive, is it permitted to sell it for that purpose (Shulḥan Arukh 153:6; Taz 4; Mishna Berura 24; Biur Halakha 13, s.v. 'Lo yimkeru'; Sha'ar Ha-Tziyun 15-18; above 9:8).

When a synagogue has a Torah scroll that is not read from, the representatives of the community may lend it or give it as a gift to another synagogue so that they will read from it, for there is no lowering of its holiness in this (Rema 153:11; Mishna Berura 68).

notes_en.en:
The law of a change to the same holiness: Megilla (27a): "They asked: What is the law of selling an old Torah scroll in order to buy a new one with it? Since one is not raising it – is it forbidden? Or perhaps, since there is no higher level to raise it to – it is permitted?". According to many one should be stringent because of the doubt (Ran on the Rif, Megilla 7b; Tur and Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 270:1; and the Shakh there 3). And some are lenient (Rabbeinu Manoaḥ, and Ha-Me'orot, Megilla 25b). And if one already sold a Torah scroll – he should buy another Torah scroll with it, since it is not possible to raise the proceeds higher (Gemara there).
According to many, only concerning a Torah scroll, above which there is no level, was the Gemara in doubt whether it is permitted to sell it in order to buy a new one in its place; but concerning other objects of holiness – it is forbidden (Ha-Ma'or and the Ran, Megilla 7a, in the name of Rabbeinu Efrayim; Ha-Hashlama and Ha-Mikhtam on Megilla chapter 3). And some say that after the fact, if one already sold, it is permitted in case of need to buy objects of the same level of holiness (Me'iri, Megilla 25b; Mahari Abuhav). Both views were brought in the Shulḥan Arukh (Oraḥ Ḥayim 153:4), and since the law is rabbinic, most Aḥaronim decided to be lenient in a situation where one already sold (Peri Megadim, Mishbetzot Zahav 1; Maḥazik Berakha 153:1; Yeḥaveh Da'at 7:26). And if it is done by the seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town, all agree that they may sell a synagogue in order to buy a finer synagogue (Responsa Benei Yehuda, Ayash 12; Oraḥ Mishpat, Oraḥ Ḥayim 151). And some are more lenient, and in their view only a Torah scroll, because of its honour, may not be sold in order to buy a new Torah scroll with it, but other holy objects may be sold for the purchase of the same level of holiness (Tosafot Yom Tov, Megilla 3:1; Magen Avraham 153:4; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 153:8; Sho'el Ve-Nish'al, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:17. And see Rashba, Megilla 25b; 27a). And since the law is rabbinic, in case of need one may rely on them.
From the plain meaning of the words of the Gemara we learned that one should not sell a Torah scroll even in order to buy with its proceeds a more mehudar Torah scroll, for the new one is by nature more mehudar, and despite this they ruled to forbid it, since there is a certain disgrace in the sale (Responsa of the Ritva 188; Taz 153:1; Ḥatam Sofer, Yoreh De'ah 254; Maharsham 6:3). And some hold that if the new one is more mehudar than the old – it is permitted, on condition that there is no concern that a mishap will occur and they will not buy the new one (Even Ha-Shoham 23; Beit David, Yoreh De'ah 139; Birkei Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 270:5. And see Pitḥei Teshuva 270:6).

sections.title_en: 6. Selling a Synagogue and 'the Seven Good Men of the Town'
sections.body_en:
It is permitted to sell a synagogue in which people no longer pray, for example when they built another, larger synagogue in its place, or when two communities united and one of the synagogues was left deserted.

The money received for the synagogue remains in the holiness of its purpose, and with it one must buy things holier than a synagogue. In case of need it is permitted to use it also for buying a synagogue or for its upkeep (Shulḥan Arukh 153:4; Mishpetei Shmuel 14; Mishna Berura 11, and as explained in the previous halakha).

After the sale, the holiness lapses from the synagogue building and it becomes ḥullin, and the buyer may use it as he wishes, on condition that he does not use it for things that involve great disgrace or have a strong stench, such as public toilets, a swimming pool or a place for tanning hides (Megilla 27b; Shulḥan Arukh 153:9). Likewise, the buyer is permitted to demolish the synagogue building and build a new building in its place, and likewise it is permitted to plant trees or bushes in its place. But it is forbidden to sow its ground, for sowing involves ploughing, which disgraces the site of the synagogue (Megilla 26b; Magen Avraham 153:37).

In a pressing situation, when there is no buyer interested in buying the deserted synagogue except a buyer who intends to use it for disgraceful uses, or when the community has a great need to use the money they will receive for it for public needs that are not sanctified – they may do so by the decision of the community's leaders and with the consent of the whole public, who are considered like 'the seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town' (Megilla 26a; Shulḥan Arukh 153:7). And then it will be permitted to sell the synagogue even for disgraceful uses, and they will likewise be permitted to use the money also for public needs that are not sanctified.

'The seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town' represent the whole public. For the seven good men of the town are the people whom the townspeople agreed to appoint as leaders to manage all their affairs. Alternatively, if the people of the community agreed that certain gabbaim would be responsible for the synagogue, in everything connected with the synagogue they have the authority of 'the good men of the town'. And there is no need for them to be seven, for only for the leadership of all the affairs of the town was it customary that there be no fewer than seven; but for the leadership of a particular matter, as long as the people of the place agreed that certain gabbaim would manage it – their law is like that of 'the good men of the town'.

The further condition is that the sale be 'in the presence of the people of the town', that is, that the decision of 'the good men of the town' be made at a general assembly of the people of the town or be publicised, in such a way that each of the townspeople can oppose the decision and try to persuade the majority of the public and the leaders to change their decision (Rashba 1:617; Maharashdam 175; Rema 153:7; Mishna Berura 29).

Today, concerning the sale of a synagogue, the leaders of the synagogue who are responsible for all its affairs are considered 'the good men of the town', including the members of the association (amuta) and the permanent gabbaim. When the municipality or the leadership of the settlement has authority over the synagogue, they must be partners in the decision. In order for the decision to be considered 'in the presence of the people of the town', the gabbaim must publicise the decision to all who attend the synagogue, so that they can appeal against their decision. In public institutions, such as yeshivot, the decision of the association is considered the decision of 'the good men of the town', and they must publicise their decision to all who are connected with the yeshiva, so that they can appeal against their decision.9

notes_en.en:
Concerning the sale of a synagogue, the Sages said in the Mishna (Megilla 27b): "They may sell it as a permanent sale, except for four things: for a bathhouse, for a tannery, for immersion, and for a 'house of water' (a lavatory)". And the same is the law for other clearly disgraceful things, such as sowing the place (there 26b, and the Rosh 1), or making a cattle barn (Taz 151:4). However, it is explained in the Gemara (there 26a) that if they sell the synagogue through "the seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town", it will be permitted to use it even for disgraceful things. Thus it is within their authority to sell the synagogue for any use. And so wrote the Rambam (Prayer 11:17), the Rosh, the Tur and the Shulḥan Arukh (153:9). And some are stringent and hold that they have the power to permit sowing on the site of a ruined synagogue, but not to use it for clearly disgraceful things (Ra'avad; Tashbetz 2:170), and ideally, when possible, we are concerned for their view (see Maharam of Lublin 59; Biur Halakha 153:9, s.v. 'Ve-im').
Similarly, in a pressing situation, for a very great need, the seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town may determine that the money received for the synagogue will be used for weekday needs (Shulḥan Arukh 153:7). According to the Ramban (Megilla 25b), this is because in truth the synagogue is considered an object of mitzva, which has no holiness, and therefore when they stop praying in it, by the letter of the law it is permitted to use it for weekday needs. But without the consent of the seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town, the people of the town are not comfortable giving up their place of mitzva and taking the money out to ḥullin. And so wrote the Rashba and the Ritva there. And according to the view of the Ran (on the Rif 8a), since the synagogue is intended for saying devarim she-bi-kedusha, "the Sages imposed holiness on it by their words". But through its sale by the seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town, its holiness lapses, because it was sanctified on the understanding that they would have the power to decide to permit it for any use, and to decide that the money received for it would go out to ḥullin (Me'iri; Biur Halakha 154:3, s.v. 'Tashmishei'). Even after the sale, the seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town may decide to take out to ḥullin the money they received for it, as emerges from the words of the Ramban, the Ritva and the Shulḥan Arukh 153:7 (Biur Halakha there, s.v. 'Aval').
As brought above, the leaders of the synagogue are considered 'the good men of the town' (Divrei Malkiel 5:11; Har Tzvi, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:76). The decision depends on the majority of the leaders and the majority of the public, for it is accepted that in all decisions one follows the majority (Ramban, Megilla 25b, s.v. 'U-shema'inan'; Divrei Malkiel 5:11; see Biur Halakha 153:7, s.v. 'Ve-hu ha-din'; and Ḥatam Sofer, Ḥoshen Mishpat 61; 116).
The gabbaim of the synagogue may annul the holiness of the synagogue by building a new synagogue in its place (Mas'at Binyamin 33; Magen Avraham 153:27). Likewise, they can annul its holiness by transferring the holiness of the synagogue onto money that they give in its place, like a sale. And here too, in a pressing situation the seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town can annul the holiness from the money (Ḥatam Sofer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 38; Avnei Nezer, Oraḥ Ḥayim 34; Heikhal Yitzḥak, Oraḥ Ḥayim 13; Minḥat Shlomo 2:4). (Some learned from the words of the Ramban that it is not possible to annul the holiness of the synagogue by transfer, but only by sale; see Har Tzvi, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:76-77; Le-Horot Natan 3:7.)

sections.title_en: 7. A Synagogue of Large Cities and a Deserted Synagogue
sections.body_en:
The permission to sell a synagogue is on condition that it is an ordinary synagogue, which belongs to the members of the community who pray in it, and consequently it is within their authority to sell it. But if it is 'a synagogue of large cities' (beit knesset shel kerakhim), that is, a rare and special synagogue situated in a central city, which serves very many Jews from all ends of the land who pray in it frequently – since the money they donated for its establishment was donated for the sake of all Jews, 'the seven good men of the town' together with all the people of that town do not have the power to sell it. And if they sold it – their sale is void, for they do not represent all the Jews to whom the synagogue belongs (Megilla 26a; Rambam, Beit Yosef and Shulḥan Arukh 153:7). However, if the members of the community needed the site of the synagogue, they are permitted to build another synagogue as good as it, and afterwards they may sell the old one, because in this way there is no harm to all those who pray in it (Mas'at Binyamin 33; Magen Avraham; Mishna Berura 153:41).

If times have changed, and 'the synagogue of large cities' has been left deserted without a minyan of worshippers, since in practice it does not function as a synagogue, the representatives of the community are permitted to sell it (Mabit 3:143; Magen Avraham 153:12). And they must use the money received for it for buying or building a synagogue in a place where a large public needs it, or for other holy needs that many require.10

Selling synagogues abroad: A neighbourhood that has been emptied of its Jewish residents, and its synagogue has been left deserted of worshippers – one should sell the deserted synagogue in order to buy or build in its place another synagogue in a place where it is needed. And those who remain in the neighbourhood or the city do not have the status of 'the good men of the town' to decide to use the money for other public needs.

In addition, one must stipulate with the buyer that he will not use the synagogue for disgraceful uses. When this demand holds up the sale, the proper representatives of the community that ceased to exist are permitted to sell it to a gentile without restriction, for in this matter they are in the place of 'the good men of the town'. When representatives of a foreign religion are the only buyers prepared to pay the value of the synagogue, because only they, for the sake of their worship, need such a large building, it is permitted in a pressing situation to sell the synagogue to a gentile real-estate dealer, and he will sell it to the highest bidder (see Mishpetei Uziel 1:4; 8:15; Beit Ridbaz 12; Igrot Moshe, Oraḥ Ḥayim 3:28. And not like the Beit Avi 3:33).11

notes_en.en:
Even though all the donors to the synagogue of large cities were from the townspeople, the good men of the town do not have authority to sell it, because it was built also for the benefit of Jews who are not from the townspeople (Rambam, Prayer 11:16; Tur and Shulḥan Arukh 153:7). And some say that its stringency stems from the fact that some of the donors are not from the townspeople, and consequently the good men of the town do not represent them (Ra'avya, Megilla 590; Or Zarua 2:385).
'A synagogue of large cities' is a rare synagogue, for only if multitudes of Jews visit it from all ends of the land is it considered 'of large cities'. Generally it existed in central commercial cities. And so wrote the Arukh Ha-Shulḥan (153:24), that synagogues of large cities are very few (in the Responsa Penei Yehoshua, Oraḥ Ḥayim 7, he wrote that in a synagogue of large cities there should generally be ten batlanim from the wider world; see Yabi'a Omer part 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 10). When the leaders of the place have great authority, and it is known to all that it was with their understanding that they donated and built the synagogue, even when it functions as a synagogue of large cities and is still active, they are permitted to sell it (Megilla 25b; Mas'at Binyamin 33; Magen Avraham 153:37).

Synagogues of large cities that became deserted, and likewise ordinary synagogues that became deserted – the few worshippers who remained there do not have the status of 'the good men of the town', and therefore they are obligated to use the money they receive for the sale of the synagogue for holy needs (Mishpetei Uziel 1, Oraḥ Ḥayim 4; Har Tzvi, Oraḥ Ḥayim 1:80, and not like the Maharshag 2:3). And so as not to hold up the sale, in a pressing situation the representatives of the community who remained there may sell it without stipulating that the buyer will not use it for disgraceful uses, for in this matter alone they are considered the seven good men of the town in the presence of the people of the town. But all this is in order to help synagogues in places that need them; under no circumstances did it occur to the builders of the synagogue and its worshippers that the few people who remained there would be considered 'the good men of the town' and 'the people of the town' to use the money from the sale of the synagogue for their own public needs.

sections.title_en: 8. The Rules of Objects of Holiness and Objects of Mitzva
sections.body_en:
The Sages said (Megilla 26b): 'Objects of mitzva' (tashmishei mitzva) are thrown away and do not require geniza, and 'objects of holiness' (tashmishei kedusha) require geniza. Let us explain the concepts:

'Objects of mitzva' are things with which a mitzva is performed, such as a sukka, a lulav, a shofar and tzitzit. And since there are no holy Names in them – they have no holiness, and after one has finished performing the mitzva with them it is permitted to use them for weekday needs that are not degrading, and there is no need to put them in geniza, provided that they are not thrown away disrespectfully (as explained above 1:11, note 14).

'Holy things' (divrei kedusha) are sacred writings that contain holy Names (above 11:1). Included in this are Torah scrolls, the passages of tefillin and mezuza, and likewise printed Ḥumashim and siddurim (above 11:7, levels 1 and 2).

'Objects of holiness' are things intended to guard the holy things with honour, or to add beauty to them, such as a mantle or bells of a Torah scroll, or the binding of a printed sacred book. And likewise things intended to serve the holiness, such as the straps of tefillin with which the tefillin are tied. In halakha, 'objects of holiness' too are considered like holy things, and therefore it is forbidden to use them for weekday needs, and after they wear out they must be put in geniza.

'An object serving an object of holiness' (tashmish de-tashmish kedusha) is a thing that serves the objects of holiness, such as a case in which the bells of the Torah scroll are stored. Its law is like 'objects of mitzva': it is permitted to use it for a weekday purpose, and after it wears out it does not require geniza, but one should not disgrace it (Mishna Berura 154:6)12

'Objects of holiness' become sanctified only through a combination of designation and an act, and one of them alone is not enough (Shulḥan Arukh, Oraḥ Ḥayim 42:3). Therefore, if they designated a bima for reading the Torah on it, as long as no act was done with it, that is, they did not use it for its sanctified use – it still has no holiness. And only after they read the Torah on it once will it rise to the level of 'an object of holiness'. If they temporarily took a table to read the Torah on it, since they did not designate it to serve permanently as a bima, even though they did an act of using it for the Torah reading – it was not sanctified (Taz 154:7).

notes_en.en: It is permitted to use 'an object serving an object of holiness' for weekday needs, as the Peri Megadim (153, Mishbetzot Zahav 15) and the Mishna Berura (154:6) wrote. However, if it is one of the objects of the synagogue, such as a parokhet, as long as it is in use – its law is like the synagogue and 'an object of holiness', and after they have finished using it, its law is like objects of mitzva (Terumat Ha-Deshen, Pesakim U-Khetavim 225; Responsa of the Baḥ 17; Peri Megadim there. And not as was learned in Piskei Teshuvot 154, 34-36, and in Halakha Berura 154, Sha'ar Ha-Tziyun 7, from the words of Da'at Torah 154:3).

sections.title_en: 9. Between 'an Object of Holiness' and 'an Object Serving an Object of Holiness'
sections.body_en:
Generally the division between 'objects of holiness' and 'an object serving an object of holiness' is that 'objects of holiness' touch the holiness itself, and therefore their law is like that of the holiness and they require geniza; whereas 'an object serving an object' does not touch the holiness itself, and from this it follows that it is not designated solely for the honour of the holiness, and therefore it has no holiness and does not require geniza.

Therefore, 'objects of holiness' that require geniza are: the 'atzei ḥayim' (rollers) around which the sheets of the Torah scroll are wound, the binder and the mantle of the scroll (according to the custom of those of Ashkenazi origin and some of those of Sephardi origin), and likewise the small ark in which the Torah scroll is held (the tik) and the cloths that go with it (according to the custom of those of Sephardi origin). But the Holy Ark, and likewise the parokhet of the Holy Ark, since they do not directly touch the Torah scroll, are 'an object serving an object of holiness', and do not require geniza.

Similarly, the bindings of printed sacred books are considered 'objects of holiness' and require geniza like the books, whereas the bookcase in which the books are placed, since it does not directly touch the pages of the books, is considered 'an object serving an object of holiness' and does not require geniza.

But a thing whose whole purpose is only for the honour of the sacred writings, even though it does not touch them, has the law of 'objects of holiness'. Therefore, a Torah crown, bells and silver rimonim, although they touch the rollers of the Torah scroll or the tik, and not the sheets of the scroll themselves, since their whole purpose is to honour the Torah and adorn it, have the law of 'objects of holiness' (Shulḥan Arukh, Yoreh De'ah 282:16). And likewise the law of a silver pointer (yad) intended for beauty and for marking the place of the reading (Magen Avraham 154:14; Mishna Berura 31).

Seemingly, according to this, the Holy Ark and the parokhet are intended for the beauty of the Torah, and should have been considered 'objects of holiness'. However, since they are intended also for the beauty of the synagogue, their law is determined according to their degree of closeness to the Torah scroll, and since they do not touch the parchment of the Torah scroll, they are 'an object serving an object of holiness' and their law is like 'objects of mitzva'.13

notes_en.en:
Megilla (26b): "Rava said: At first I would say that this kursya is an object serving an object, and is permitted. Once I saw that they place a Torah scroll on it, I said: it is an object of holiness, and forbidden". Rashi explained that the 'kursya' is the bima on which the Torah scroll is placed, and at first Rava held that it does not have the law of 'an object of holiness' because a cloth is spread over it, and if so the cloth is 'an object of holiness' and the bima 'an object serving an object'. However, when he saw that sometimes the Torah scroll is placed directly on the bima, he decided that it has the law of 'an object of holiness'. It is implied that only what touches the holiness has the law of 'an object of holiness'. Rabbeinu Yeruḥam added (Toledot Adam Ve-Ḥava 2:4) that things whose whole purpose is for the honour of the Torah scroll, even when they do not touch the scroll itself, are 'objects of holiness', and his words are accepted in halakha (Beit Yosef, Oraḥ Ḥayim 154:8; Peri Megadim 154, Eshel Avraham 8; Mishna Berura 154:14, and others).
Parokhet: its law is like 'an object serving an object', since it does not touch the Torah scroll, but serves as a partition for the Holy Ark (Responsa Maharam Padua 82; Responsa of the Baḥ, Ha-Yeshanot 17; Magen Avraham 154:8; Eliya Rabba 5; Peri Megadim, Eshel Avraham 8; Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 3; Mishna Berura 14). But its law is like that of the synagogue (Rema 154:6); therefore, while it serves its purpose, its law is like an object of holiness, but when they stop using it for its purpose, it has no holiness (as explained above, note 12). And likewise the law of the Holy Ark customary in our days: since it does not touch the books directly, and it is intended also for the honour of the synagogue, as explained above – its holiness is like the holiness of a synagogue (Erekh Leḥem 282:12; Perisha, Yoreh De'ah 282:17; Baḥ 7; Korban Netanel, Megilla 4:2:1; Yabi'a Omer part 8, Oraḥ Ḥayim 19:14-17). However, some say that the Holy Ark is 'an object of holiness', as they said in Megilla (26b) concerning 'deluskamei sefarim' (book chests), and likewise concerning a 'teivuta' (an ark). And even though the ark does not actually touch the Torah scroll, in their view it is intended for its honour (Gra, Yoreh De'ah 282:28; Rav Pe'alim part 2, Oraḥ Ḥayim 20; Yaskil Avdi 7, Oraḥ Ḥayim 7; Tzitz Eliezer 18:7). In their view, the reason people are lenient to place in the Holy Ark also less holy things is that this is the custom, and consequently it is considered as though they stipulated so. Similarly one can say that they also stipulated not to put it in geniza. However, it appears more likely that the ark spoken of in the Gemara was small and held the Torah scroll alone, and it was clear that all its beauty was for the honour of the Torah scroll. This is not so with the Holy Arks of our days, which are large and designed in a way that suits the synagogue, and therefore they do not have the law of 'objects of holiness' (similarly wrote the Melamed Le-Ho'il 1:18). If inside the ark there is a locked frame intended to guard the books from thieves, the law of this frame is like that of a thing intended only for guarding, which has no holiness, as the Rema wrote 154:3 (below note 15).

sections.title_en: 10. The Bima, the Mezuza Case and the Tefillin Bag
sections.body_en:
It is forbidden to place printed sacred books on the bima that serves for the Torah reading, and likewise it is forbidden to lean on it, since it is sanctified for placing the Torah scroll. However, if they stipulated from the outset concerning the bima that it would be permitted to use it also for weekday needs, even though it is considered 'an object of holiness', it is permitted to use it for weekday needs, as they stipulated, on condition that the bima is not disgraced thereby. Not only this, but in a place where it is known that people are accustomed to place printed sacred books on the bima, this is permitted even without their having stipulated so explicitly, for everyone knows that it was on this understanding that they consecrated the bima. And likewise is the law with all objects of holiness: it is possible to limit the taking effect of holiness by a stipulation, and likewise the custom of the public is considered like a stipulation (Shulḥan Arukh and Rema 154:8; Mishna Berura 33-34). Therefore, since it was not customary to put the bima in geniza after its use – there is no need to put it in geniza; it suffices to take care not to discard it disrespectfully. But the cloth on it, or the glass covering over the cloth, must be put in geniza.14

A mezuza case, even though the nylon that wraps the mezuza separates between it and the mezuza, since its whole purpose is to add honour and beauty to the mezuza, is 'an object of holiness'. But the nylon in which the mezuza is wrapped to prevent mould does not require geniza, since it is intended only for protection and not for honour.15

The leather housings (batim) of the tefillin, in which the passages always lie – are considered 'holy things', since they are an inseparable part of the tefillin (Sha'ar Ha-Tziyun 154:7). Therefore, the plastic boxes in which people usually keep the batim are considered 'objects of holiness' and require geniza. And the bag in which they are placed is 'an object serving an object', and has no holiness, and therefore it is permitted to put a siddur, a mirror and weekday things in it, and there is no need to put it in geniza. The straps of the tefillin are considered 'objects of holiness' (Megilla 26b; Shulḥan Arukh 154:3).16

notes_en.en:
The bima, which is called in the Gemara 'kursya', is considered 'an object of holiness' even when it is covered with a cloth (Megilla 26b; Shulḥan Arukh 154:3; Mishna Berura 10). According to many this is because sometimes the cloth is removed and the Torah scroll is placed on the bima. Consequently, if the bima is always covered with a cloth, or the scroll always rests in its tik as is the custom of those of Sephardi origin, the bima has no holiness (as explained in the previous note according to Rashi; and so wrote the Rosh, Megilla 4:11; the Mordekhai; Rabbeinu Yeruḥam 2:4; Beit Yosef 154:8; Darkhei Moshe 1*; Magen Avraham 6; Kaf Ha-Ḥayim 22). And some say that even when the bima is always covered with a cloth it has holiness, because it supports the Torah scroll, and the cloth is subordinate to it (Rabbi Avraham Min Ha-Har; Rishon Le-Tziyon and Sefat Emet on Megilla 26b; Ben Yedid and Rav Kafiḥ on the Rambam, Torah Scroll 10:4).
Seemingly there is a difficulty with the prevalent custom of placing on the bima and on the cloth over it things of mitzva, such as the requirements for havdala and lists of those called up, and even printed books whose level of holiness is not like that of a Torah scroll; but since they stipulated so – it is permitted (Yerushalmi Megilla 3:1; Ra'avya, Megilla 590; Mordekhai, Megilla 820; Rosh 4:1; Shulḥan Arukh 154:8). And even if they did not stipulate explicitly, since it is accepted to use the bima for these objects of mitzva, and likewise to knock on it when necessary to quieten the public, it is as though they stipulated explicitly (Terumat Ha-Deshen 273; Beit Yosef and Rema 154:8; Beit Yehuda, Oraḥ Ḥayim 27). And it is better to stipulate explicitly (Magen Avraham 154:15). In any event one should not use the bima for degrading uses, such as placing dirty papers on it or sitting on it (Mishna Berura 154:34). A stipulation is effective for 'objects of holiness' and not for the holiness itself (Peri Megadim, Mishbetzot Zahav 154:7). (More on the stipulation, see above 12, note 7.)

Megilla (26b): "Rava said: These baskets for Ḥumashim and these chests for books (boxes in which the books are kept) – are objects of holiness, and are put in geniza. That is obvious! You might have said: these are not made for honour, they are made merely for protection – so it teaches us". Thus anything intended only for protection is not 'an object of holiness'. And so explained R. Yehonatan of Lunel and the Nimukei Yosef there. And so ruled the Or Zarua (2:386), the Mordekhai (822), the Beit Yosef (154:6) and others. Thus what touches the holiness, as long as it is also for the sake of honour – is 'an object of holiness', and if it is only for the sake of protection – it is not 'an object of holiness'. And if it does not touch but is intended only for honour, like a silver Torah crown – it is considered 'an object of holiness' (Peri Megadim, Eshel Avraham 8; Mishna Berura 14; and as in the words of Rabbeinu Yeruḥam above, note 13). (And according to the Me'iri, Megilla 26b, even what is intended only for protection is considered 'an object of holiness'. And one can still argue that even in his view the case is of a protector that also adds a little honour, but the nylon in which the mezuza is wrapped has not a trace of honour in it, and according to all views it does not require geniza. And see Avnei Yashfeh 5:25; Ohel Ya'akov 4:21.)

The straps of the tefillin are 'objects of holiness' (baraita, Megilla 26b). Tosafot learned from this (there, s.v. 'Tashmishei') that the knots in the shape of yod and dalet on the straps are not complete letters of the Name 'Shaddai', and therefore the straps are 'objects of holiness' and not 'holy things'. And they raised a difficulty against Rashi (Menaḥot 35b, s.v. 'Shin of Hashem'), who wrote that these letters are part of the Name 'Shaddai', and it is implied that according to his view the straps have intrinsic holiness, as the Baḥ explained (154:1). And some hold that even according to Rashi the straps are only 'objects of holiness' (see Ran, Shabbat 62a; Ritva, Shabbat 28b). In practice, the view of most poskim is that the straps are 'objects of holiness' (Shulḥan Arukh 154:3; Taz 2; Olat Tamid 5; Magen Avraham 42:6; Eliya Rabba 4; Biur Halakha, s.v. 'Le-guf ha-kedusha'). According to this, the plastic boxes that protect the batim of the tefillin, if there is in them an addition for beauty and honour, are 'objects of holiness', and the bag in which they are placed is 'an object serving an object', which is not holy, and it is permitted to put weekday things in it (Biur Halakha 34:4, s.v. 'Shtei ha-zugot'). And some are stringent and are concerned for the view of Rashi as Tosafot understood it, and then the bag in which the tefillin and straps are placed is 'an object of holiness', and only in the tallit bag is it permitted to put weekday things (Magen Giborim 154:3; Piskei Teshuvot 154:6). But even according to them, if one stipulated in advance that he would put a mirror or a siddur in the tefillin bag, or this is the custom in his family, the stipulation is effective (Beit Yosef 42:2; Rema there 3).
Tefillin that wore out – one puts the batim with the passages in geniza in earthenware vessels near the grave of a Torah scholar (Arukh Ha-Shulḥan 282:16; Marḥeshet 1:53). Today there are special compartments in geniza containers for tefillin and mezuzot. And if the batim have been separated from the passages, simply, the batim do not require stringent geniza. And some are stringent with the head tefillin, since it has a 'shin' on it (see Peri Megadim, Mishbetzot Zahav 154:2; Sha'ar Ha-Tziyun 7; Ginzei Ha-Kodesh 6:6).
